Executing experimental tasks in both normal research laboratories and
large-scale scientific facilities often requires extensive human supervision
and remains a key challenge on the path to fully autonomous, artificial
intelligence (AI)-driven science. Here we demonstrate a large language
model-driven agent that autonomously performs X-ray sample alignment
on a synchrotron beamline by planning actions, executing instrumental
commands, interpreting observations and iterating towards experimental
goals. Based on existing large language models with structured tool-use via
the model context protocol, our AI X-ray scientist was guided and tested
using an in-house-built virtual experimental setup that mirrors a six-circle
diffractometer at an operational synchrotron beamline. The agentic
workflow developed in the virtual environment was directly deployed on
a real beamline, where it correctly identified reference reflections and
determined the orientation matrix, an essential first step in any type of
single-crystal scattering experiment. Our AI X-ray scientist responded
effectively to unexpected experimental conditions, demonstrating adaptive
problem-solving and readiness for addressing practical experimental
situations. Our study provides a step towards autonomous operation across
diverse experimental environments at large-scale scattering facilities.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming scientific research
by accelerating simulations, predicting molecular and material
structures and facilitating knowledge extraction from experimental
data1–8. Although the long-term vision of autonomous scientific
discovery is widely anticipated, wherein AI will not only analyse
data but also plan and execute physical experiments, concrete
progress towards this goal remains challenging in large scientific
research infrastructures.
Recent studies have demonstrated promising applications of
AI including machine learning and large language models (LLMs)
in autonomous scientific discovery, such as Bayesian experimen-
tal design and active learning9–19, reinforcement-learning materials
designers and experimental controllers20–23 and robotic diffractometer
alignment21,24,25, as well as LLM-assisted scientific reasoning and agentic
laboratory workflows14,26–38. In parallel, advances in embodied AI and
robotics have enabled systems capable of executing complex physical

layer that autonomously sequences, interprets and adapts experimental
actions through iterative tool use rather than executing a fixed pre-
scripted workflow. Here, we present our methodology for developing an
AI-driven X-ray scientist based on agentic LLM reasoning and structured
tool use and demonstrate its deployment on a real X-ray beamline at the
Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL) at SLAC National
Accelerator Laboratory. Rather than presenting new learning mecha-
nisms or agentic AI architectures, this study centres on the development
and deployment of existing reasoning-capable LLMs for closed-loop
execution of a concrete experimental task at a synchrotron facility.
A key challenge in this development lies in exposing the agentic
AI to real-world experimental environments and situations. As facility
beamlines are complex and often oversubscribed, and experimental
conditions can be very different from simulated conditions due to imper-
fections (for example, noise, spurious signals and technical limitations)
and safety considerations (for example, radiation hazards and risks of
motor collisions), making training an AI X-ray scientist directly from
scratch on physical instruments impractical. Therefore, we developed
a virtual beamline that replicated essential experimental operations and
allowed our agentic AI to directly interact with it to perform simulated
experiments. This enabled us to prepare our AI X-ray scientist in a virtual
experimental environment before transitioning to a real experiment.
We showcase the capabilities of our AI X-ray scientist by asking it to
determine the orientation matrix of a randomly aligned single-crystal
sample, which is an essential and demanding prerequisite in many types
of scattering experiments. This task involves navigation in reciprocal
space using multiple degrees of freedom, often under strict physical
constraints of motor limits and safety interlocks. Additional complica-
tions arising from unexpected situations such as hidden motor offsets,
imperfect centres of rotation and uneven sample mounting can make
the process even more challenging. Incomplete or missing information
on residual stresses and the in-plane orientation of the sample69, as well
as motor position reproducibility issues, can require human experts
to undertake time-consuming trial-and-error procedures. For all these
reasons, single-crystal sample alignment serves as an ideal testbed for
evaluating the capabilities of our AI X-ray scientist.
We first introduce the overall workflow and guidance framework
for AI X-ray scientists, followed by demonstrations in both virtual and
real-beamline environments. We then benchmark multiple agentic
AI models on orientation estimation and lattice parameter predic-
tion tasks and finally demonstrate autonomous sample alignment at
SSRL, including adaptation to unexpected motor offsets during real
experimental operation.
Results
Agentic AI-driven X-ray experimentation
Our agentic AI X-ray scientist was informed by physical knowledge and
equipped with the necessary experimental tools via an MCP framework
(‘MCP server and tools’ section in Methods). As illustrated in Fig. 1a,
the AI X-ray scientist is granted access to terminal input/output his-
tory, detector images and motor scan results. We adopt the setup of a
six-circle diffractometer70, a widely used and highly flexible instrument
configuration. It includes six degrees of freedom: two detector motors
(δ and ν) and four sample motors (ϕ, χ, η and μ).
Within this framework, the AI X-ray scientist could issue beamline
commands, such as those used by the X-ray instrument control software
SPEC71, to operate the diffractometer. After a command is issued and
executed, the AI X-ray scientist may check the experimental status or
results, reason about the next steps and repeat this process until the
experimental goal is achieved. A list of commands that the AI X-ray sci-
entist can use is given in Table 1. In virtual experiments using the beam-
line simulator, all steps are carried out automatically by the AI X-ray
scientist without human intervention, including command execution
and results analysis. However, for the first real-beamline demonstration
on BL17-2 at SSRL, the AI X-ray scientist autonomously generated the
tasks in real-world environments39–41. These developments signal the
feasibility of AI systems that interact with the physical world. Further
advances in LLMs, particularly those with enhanced reasoning capabili-
ties and the ability to use tools via the model context protocol (MCP)
have enabled the emergence of powerful agentic AI systems42–47 with the
ability to think, reason and use external tools for addressing complex
scientific problems48,49. Building on this foundation, a growing body
of work has begun applying agentic AI systems to perform real-world
experiments across chemistry, biology and materials science30–38.
These recent advances in agentic AI-driven experimentation in
real-world settings bring hope for achieving autonomous physical rea-
soning and operation in large-scale research facilities, such as the X-ray,
neutron and electron scattering facilities25,50–54. These facilities have
been playing a foundational role in scientific discovery across materials
science, chemistry, biology and physics7,55–65. However, these facilities
are highly oversubscribed and require substantial human expertise for
experimental operation. Meanwhile, increasing experimental com-
plexity and major facility upgrades, including LCLS-II (Linac Coherent
Light Source II) and the Advanced Photon Source Upgrade66–68, further
intensify demands on beamtime efficiency and expert-driven operation.
Although many individual beamline operations can be addressed
using deterministic optimization or scripted automation, real experi-
mental workflows often require coordinating multiple steps under
uncertainty, incomplete information and unexpected outcomes. Agentic
AI systems offer a promising solution by serving as a flexible reasoning

In silico development and validation
We leverage in-context learning capabilities of agentic AI models72,73,
where the preparation of guidance prompts play a central role. Given the
limited availability of real beamtime, all guidance and testing were con-
ducted using our in-house virtual beamline simulator (see ‘Virtual beam-
line for simulated experiments’ section in Methods for more details).
The overall sample alignment workflow provided in the guid-
ance is summarized in Fig. 1b, consisting of the following major steps:
(1) setup: the AI X-ray scientist acquires basic instrument and sample
information, including the X-ray wavelength, lattice parameters and
a list of accessible reflections. (2) Primary reflection search and opti-
mization: the agent first moves to the theoretically calculated motor
positions based on the target reflection’s 2θ angle and then performs
one or more rounds of scans over η, χ and δ to optimize peak intensity
and centre the Bragg peak; the motors μ and ν are not used, given the
vertical reflection geometry (Fig. 1a). (3) Secondary reflection search
and optimization: this step is similar to the previous step but with the
added challenge of resolving in-plane orientation, often requiring a suf-
ficiently wide ϕ scan. Motor movements are subject to physical limits
(defined in Table 2), which are adopted from an operational beamline
(BL17-2 at SSRL). In the zoomed-in view of Fig. 1b, the theoretical values
for η are calculated from the sample surface normal vector n and the
scattering vector Q, for Q vectors lying in the scattering plane.
Note that the high-level workflow shown in Fig. 1b serves as a con-
ceptual scaffold rather than a hard-coded execution script. Although
the overall goal and the set of available tools are specified, the AI X-ray
scientist autonomously determines which tools to invoke, when to
transition between the stages, which reflection peaks to probe and
how to configure motor scans based on intermediate observations
and the inferred experimental state. In practice, we provide detailed
guidance prompts that describe the task structure and available tools
at a high level, analogous to instructional documentation, while leaving
all execution decisions to the AI agent (see ‘LLMs’ section of Methods
for additional details; Supplementary Note 1).
We used the magnetic Weyl semimetal Co3Sn2S2 as our example
material sample, which crystallizes in the rhombohedral space group
R̄3m (no. 166)74,75. In its conventional hexagonal cell, the lattice param-
eters are a = b ≈ 5.36 Å, c ≈ 13.02 Å and α = β = 90°, γ = 120° from the crystal
structure file obtained via the Materials Project76,77. Figure 2a shows an
example of the search and optimization process for the secondary refer-
ence reflection, (1, 0, 10), using our virtual beamline. As outlined in the
workflow, the process begins with a wide ϕ scan, during which the AI
X-ray scientist identifies a diffraction peak near ϕ ≈ −40.71°. A detector
image is then acquired to confirm the presence of the peak, followed
by an η scan to optimize its intensity. The AI X-ray scientist subsequently
initiates a centring routine by scanning over χ and δ, whose effects on
peak position are illustrated in Fig. 2a. The procedure concludes with a
final η scan and another detector image to verify successful peak opti-
mization. For each motor scan, the diffraction intensity plotted as a
function of motor position corresponds to the integrated intensity
within a specific region of interest (ROI): a vertical line ROI for χ and ϕ
scans, a horizontal line ROI for δ scans and a centre area ROI for η scans.
Note that in real experiments, it is quite rare to begin with no in-plane
orientation information. The example shown here therefore represents
a more challenging case than what is typically encountered, further
highlighting the robustness and adaptability of the AI X-ray scientist.
We note that the AI agent does not directly receive raw numerical
detector arrays or tabular scan data. Detector images are provided
to the AI agent as image inputs for qualitative interpretation. Results
from motor scans are returned through MCP tools as rendered plots,
with fitted curves and peak centres overlaid when fitting is successful,
as illustrated in Fig. 2a.
To further assess the reliability of our AI X-ray scientist in complet-
ing the alignment process, we benchmarked two LLMs, Claude
Sonnet 4 (ref. 78) and Gemini 2.5 Flash79 (see ‘LLMs’ section in Methods
for details). Each model was evaluated via ten independent runs, with

task difficulty. The following two evaluation metrics were used to

The results for AI X-ray scientist based on two different LLMs are
summarized in Fig. 2b,c. Both models successfully aligned the sample
accurately in the majority of cases, consistently making alignment
error below 5° for most runs. For runs with larger alignment errors, the
primary cause was imperfect peak centreing by the AI X-ray scientist,
for example, when adjusting the δ and χ motors. Nevertheless, in all
such cases, the agent still successfully located the peak on the detec-
tor, allowing subsequent physically meaningful measurements. Some
example detector images are provided in Supplementary Note 2. In
terms of lattice parameter estimation, each model produced highly
accurate c values, with the absolute error smaller than 0.01 Å, in more
than half of the trials. Although this level of accuracy does not yet match
the precision typically required in crystallography experiments, it is
important to note that the most challenging step is often locating the
correct peak in the first place for general experiments. Once the peak
is identified, refining lattice parameters is comparatively straightfor-
ward, although it involves some repetitive procedures. The number of
tool-use calls issued by each LLM is reported in Supplementary Note 3.
To better understand the overall performance of the agentic
AI-driven workflow under various challenging conditions, we evalu-
ate the Gemini 2.5 Flash-based AI X-ray scientist in multiple scenarios
involving larger motor offsets, multi-grain diffraction, reduced reason-
ing budgets and lower LLM sampling temperature (Fig. 2d,e). Across
these scenarios, the agent was generally able to recover the sample
orientation and lattice parameter with reasonable accuracy in suc-
cessful runs, although performance degraded under more adversarial
conditions, particularly when reasoning depth was restricted. Repre-
sentative examples and additional analyses, including failure modes
associated with motor-limit behaviour and multi-grain peak fitting,
are provided in Supplementary Notes 4 and 5. These results suggest
that the workflow remains reasonably robust under imperfect and
non-ideal experimental conditions.
Deploying the AI X-ray scientist on a real synchrotron
experiment
The successful application of the AI X-ray scientist in virtual experiments
is promising; however, real-world validation is an essential step given the
presence of sample imperfections, instrument variability, safety con-
straints, observation noise and other factors not captured in simulation.
In this section, we demonstrate that the AI X-ray scientist can perform
autonomous tasks on a real hard X-ray beamline while retaining its core
agentic workflow, requiring only necessary interface-level adaptations
to accommodate the real-beamline experimental data stream.
We deployed the AI X-ray scientist on beamline BL17-2 at SSRL.
Details about real experiments are presented in Methods section (Syn-
chrotron X-ray experiment) and Supplementary Note 6. The same
guidance used in the virtual experiments was provided, apart from
one safety-related constraint: the AI X-ray scientist was prompted
to output the terminal command it intended to run using the format
‘Execute Command: [commands]’, which was then relayed by a human
experimentalist to the controlling terminal. After each execution, the
AI was simply told ‘Please read the log and continue’. Beyond this fixed
relay step, there was no additional interaction; the human presence
served purely as a passive safety intermediary, without influencing
the experiment’s outcome or the AI’s decision-making process. All
other actions, including accessing terminal input/output histories,
analysing scan results and acquiring detector images, were carried out
independently by the AI X-ray scientist using MCP tools as detailed in
the ‘MCP server and tools’ section in Methods.
For the real-world beamline experiments, we used a more capable
model, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 478, to maximize robustness and mini-
mize operational risk during limited and valuable beamtime. Although
other tested models were also able to perform the task in simulation,
the use of a larger model was a practical choice to ensure reliability
under real experimental conditions. Due to beamtime constraints, real
experiment configurations were not systematically repeated under
identical conditions during the beamline session.
For real experimental demonstration, we used Co3Sn2S2, the same
material system considered in the virtual experiments, whereas the
AI X-ray scientist was provided with a different structure file from the
Crystallography Open Database80,81. The Crystallography Open Data-
base structure file was adopted in accord with standard experimental
practice, which favours experimentally curated crystal structures in
real measurements. This choice does not affect the agentic workflow,
which is independent of the crystallographic data source. After acquir-
ing basic experimental information during the setup phase, the AI X-ray
scientist began planning and searching for the first reference reflection,
as illustrated by the AI quote shown in Extended Data Fig. 1.
Given that Co3Sn2S2 has a hexagonal lattice with a substantially
longer c axis, the AI X-ray scientist reasonably assumes that the c axis
is aligned with the surface normal and selects a specular (0, 0, L) reflec-
tion, specifically (0, 0, 6), as the initial target. It sets the η and δ motors
to the theoretical values corresponding to this reflection and captures
a detector image, which reveals a faint peak (Fig. 3a). It then performs
a scan over η and adjusts the motor to the angle that maximizes inten-
sity (Fig. 3b). Notably, the AI agent identifies an unexpected offset of
approximately 1.22° in η, potentially caused by the uneven surface of
the copper sample holder. The AI agent highlights this deviation in its
reasoning and updates η accordingly, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 2,
showcasing its ability to adapt to experimental imperfections.
Next, the AI X-ray scientist captures another detector image to
confirm that the intensity has been successfully optimized (Fig. 3c).
It then proceeds through a centring process using χ and δ (Fig. 3d–f),
mirroring the workflow from the virtual experiments. The final η opti-
mization demonstrates the AI X-ray scientist’s ability to perform precise
and high-quality sample alignment. Finally, it acquires a verification
image (Fig. 3g) and sets the current diffractometer configuration as
the primary reference reflection using the or0 0 0 6 command.
With the primary reference reflection identified, the AI X-ray sci-
entist proceeds to locate the secondary reference reflection with the
reasoning process for planning shown in Extended Data Fig. 3. Based on
the calculated angular separation and peak intensities, the agent selects
the (1, 0, 10) reflection as a suitable candidate, noting its sufficient
intensity (7.2% of the strongest peak’s intensity) and the constraint to
prevent the scattering vector from pointing below the sample surface
(η = 2.06°). To account for the previously discovered offset in η (≈1.22°),
it adjusts the target value to η = 0.84°, while setting δ ≈ 35.72° accord-
ingly. Execution of this command successfully positions the detector
to capture the (1, 0, 10) peak (Fig. 4a). Notably, the AI X-ray scientist was
not provided with any prior information about the sample’s in-plane
orientation. Nevertheless, the peak appears even before any ϕ scan is
conducted (Fig. 4b), owing to relatively good initial sample placement
and the peak’s broad intensity distribution in the ϕ degree of freedom.
The AI X-ray scientist eventually identifies the correct in-plane orienta-
tion near ϕ ≈ −2.88°. Importantly, the AI X-ray scientist still performs a
sufficiently wide ϕ scan that would have enabled successful alignment
even under less favourable initial conditions. As shown in Fig. 4c–f, the
agent carries out peak centring and intensity optimization, ultimately
converging on a well-aligned configuration for the (1, 0, 10) reflection
(Fig. 4g). Throughout this sequence, the AI scientist maintains focus
on the Bragg peak, effectively ignoring a strong diffraction ring that
appears in the detector image. The verification peak (2, 0, 14) is shown
in Supplementary Note 7 to confirm the correct alignment.
Although the encountered unexpected η offset and the corre-
sponding adaptive alignment behaviour were observed during a limited
number of real-beamline trials and should not be interpreted as a statis-
tically established capability, this result demonstrates the potential of
an LLM-driven agent to maintain robust closed-loop operation under
unmodelled experimental conditions through iterative observation
and reasoning.

We also carried out a real experimental demonstration using a
single-crystal Si sample, in which the AI X-ray scientist successfully
aligned the sample under a challenging situation involving a significant
motor offset of Δη = 1.5° and extremely sharp peaks. Further details are
provided in Supplementary Note 8. These real-world demonstrations
provide proof-of-concept evidence that the AI X-ray scientist can oper-
ate reliably and flexibly in real experimental environments and may
serve as an effective collaborator in experimental science.
Discussion
We presented a methodology for preparing an agentic AI X-ray scien-
tist through virtual experimentation and validated its performance
on a real-world synchrotron X-ray instrument. The AI X-ray scientist
demonstrated promising performance on virtual benchmarks and
successfully aligned samples in real experiments, including both a
high-quality Si crystal sample with sharp peaks and a Co3Sn2S2 sample
with broader peaks. These demonstrations across both virtual and

Rather than introducing a new learning algorithm or fine-tuning
the underlying language model, this work focuses on how
reasoning-capable LLMs can be operationalized for closed-loop experi-
mental execution on real, large-scale scientific instruments. The key
contribution is to show that, when coupled with structured tool inter-

workflows in realistic scientific settings. Although the core reasoning
model is used off the shelf, we view this as an enabling factor that lowers
the barrier to deploying general-purpose AI X-ray scientists in experi-
mental facilities and as a foundation for future work that may integrate
learning-based components on top of such agentic control frameworks.
In the meantime, although the present study focuses on sam-
ple alignment, this task represents a broadly relevant prerequisite
for many synchrotron X-ray, X-ray free electron laser and neutron
experiments. A particularly important future direction is the devel-
opment of meta-agents that can assist in constructing and refining
instrument-specific guidance prompts, thereby reducing the upfront
effort required to adapt the framework to new beamlines, instruments
and experimental workflows. Future work may further extend these
capabilities through improved tool interfaces, retrieval-augmented
reasoning, data-driven experimental planning and task-specific adap-
tation strategies17,82–86.
Taken together, our results demonstrate that agentic AI X-ray
scientists can perform meaningful tasks in real experimental settings.
We envision a future where autonomous AI systems serve not just as
tools for automation but as scientific assistants or even collaborators
that improve efficiency of complex facilities and enable entirely new
modes of experimentation. With continued development, we believe
that agentic AI holds the potential to reshape the research landscape
and greatly accelerate the pace of scientific discovery.

MCP server and tools
We developed an MCP server89 hosting the necessary tools to enable
interactions between the AI X-ray scientist and the virtual beamline. The
general workflow proceeds as follows: the AI X-ray scientist first creates
a new Python session, which maintains its own global state. Within this
session, the AI instantiates a Python object, experiment (implemented
as a Python class), representing the virtual experiment. This object
hosts the sample and diffractometer states, enabling it to mimic experi-
mental operations (for example, moving motors or performing scans)
and generate simulated detector images. The AI then issues ‘terminal
commands’ via the MCP tool execute_command. These commands are
not executed directly on a real system terminal; instead, they are parsed
by simple keyword detection and directed to trigger the corresponding
Python methods on the virtual experiment object, thereby emulating
the behaviour and workflow of the real-beamline control software.
The AI X-ray scientist can complete essential experimental operations
through the commands introduced in Table 1 using this MCP tool. Some
other auxiliary MCP tools are also made available to the AI X-ray scien-
tist, such as get_sample_information for querying the basic sample
and experimental information including lattice parameters, attainable
reflections and X-ray wavelength. In virtual experiments, the AI X-ray
scientists directly obtain results after calling an MCP tool run. In real
experiments, given the relay step of terminal commands, additional
MCP tools are prepared, including read_log, explore_directory,
read_and_plot_image and read_and_plot_spec, such that the
AI X-ray scientist can check out terminal inputs/outputs, recent file
changes, detector images and scan results.
In the current implementation, terminal command extraction
from the LLM output is performed using a keyword-based parsing strat-
egy, designed to mirror established beamline control workflows (for
example, those used in SPEC-like interfaces). Although this approach
proved sufficient for the experiments reported here, we acknowledge
that keyword-based parsing can be susceptible to ambiguity or format-
ting errors. More structured output schemes, such as enforcing JavaS-
cript Object Notation-based schemas or typed interfaces (for example,
via pydantic models), represent a promising direction for improving
robustness and reliability in future implementations.
Synchrotron X-ray experiment
The Synchrotron X-ray experiment was carried out at beamline BL17-2
of the SSRL, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The incident X-ray
energy was set to 16.0 keV, corresponding to a wavelength of around
0.7749 Å. The Co3Sn2S2 sample was mounted on a copper holder, and
measurements were performed at room temperature under ambient
air. Photographs of the sample and the six-circle diffractometer are
provided in Supplementary Note 6. We note that, during deployment
from the virtual to the real beamline, minor environment-specific
adjustments were made to MCP tools to match the real-beamline con-
trol interface; however, the AI agent’s prompting, reasoning structure
and decision logic remained unchanged.

Both agentic AI models were initialized with a combination of a
short prompt and a long guidance prompt, with the agent prompted
to ‘Please continue.’ whenever the process is interrupted such as by
reaching the maximum number of steps. The short prompt specified
essential information, such as the working directory containing the
structure file and the expected experimental outputs, along with key
reminders for the AI X-ray scientist. The long guidance prompt pro-
vided additional context and detailed instructions. More information
about these prompts is provided in Supplementary Note 1. Information
about complete conversation histories for the results presented in
deploying the AI X-ray scientist on a real synchrotron experiment can
be found in Supplementary Note 9.
Guidance prompts were primarily developed within the virtual
beamline environment. The process began with writing detailed docu-
mentation for each MCP tool, specifying its purpose, required inputs,
returned outputs and appropriate usage, often supplemented with
illustrative examples. We then provided high-level workflow guid-
ance describing the overall experimental procedure and alignment
objectives. These documents were designed to be generalizable for
accomplishing the alignment task while remaining agnostic to the
specific crystal under study.
Although the long guidance prompt provides detailed step-by-step
instructions for the workflow, execution order and control flow are not
hard-coded and are instead determined by the AI agent. Decisions such
as selecting target reference reflections and transitioning between
peak searching and refinement are autonomously determined by the AI
agent, distinguishing our approach from traditional script-based auto-
mation. Prompt preparation further involved iterative identification of
failure modes during simulated operation (for example, unreasonable
scan ranges), followed by refinements that guide the agent towards
safer and more reliable behaviours. Behaviours that were insufficiently
followed by the AI agent despite being described in the long prompt
are explicitly reiterated in the short guidance prompt.
